concept: LAG and LEAD read values from another row in a defined ordering without a self-join. LAG looks backward; LEAD looks forward. They do not automatically mean previous calendar month.
example:
WITH Monthly AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS RevenueMonth, SUM(Amount) AS Revenue
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID, DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)
)
SELECT CustomerID, RevenueMonth, Revenue,
       LAG(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY RevenueMonth) AS PriorObservedRevenue
FROM Monthly;
breakdown: The CTE creates one row per customer and observed month.
PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each customer.
ORDER BY determines which row is previous.
A missing February means March looks back to January; use a calendar table or month-aware self-join when you require the immediately preceding calendar month.
practice: Modify the query to return the next observed month’s revenue with LEAD, alongside prior observed revenue.
answer:
WITH Monthly AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS RevenueMonth, SUM(Amount) AS Revenue
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID, DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)
)
SELECT CustomerID, RevenueMonth, Revenue,
       LAG(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY RevenueMonth) AS PriorObservedRevenue,
       LEAD(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY RevenueMonth) AS NextObservedRevenue
FROM Monthly;
takeaways: LAG and LEAD work on ordered rows, not calendar intervals.
Aggregate to the intended grain before using a window function.
